sections.history: Tirukkaruppariyalur is the Tevaram name of the village now called Thalainayar, or Thalaignayiru, in the Mayiladuthurai country on the north bank of the Kaveri. The hymns of Sambandar and Sundarar praise the Lord here, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, and the Periya Puranam remembers Sambandar's visit. The village has been known by the older names Karuppariyalur and Karmanasapuram, the place where karma is undone, and because it lies west of Sirkazhi it is also called Melaikazhi. Inscriptions at the temple, about a dozen in number, belong to the reigns of Kulothunga Chola III and Rajaraja III and to a Vijayanagara ruler, and they name the place as a Brahmin settlement of the Chola country, from which the modern name Thalainayar is thought to come.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east, with the sanctum of Kutram Porutha Nathar holding a self-manifested linga, while the goddess Kolvalai Nayaki has her own shrine facing south. It is counted among the kokudi koil temples, a name linked to the kokudi, a fragrant jasmine, which is also the sacred tree of the place; the sacred water is the Indra tirtham. Accounts describe a modest Dravidian temple with shrines for Vinayaka, Murugan and Dakshinamurthy set around the sanctum, and one tradition speaks of upper shrines raised above the ground, which is why the village is called the western Sirkazhi. Exact dimensions and the form of the tower are not recorded in the sources consulted.
sections.legends: The name of the Lord tells the legend. Indra, king of the gods, once hurled his thunderbolt at a being he did not recognise, and it struck Shiva; when he understood what he had done he was overcome with remorse, and the Lord forgave him. From this the Shiva of Tirukkaruppariyalur is called Kutram Porutha Nathar, the Lord who bears with faults, or in Sanskrit Aparadha Kshameswarar, and the temple tank is named for Indra. Another tradition remembers Hanuman, who coiled his tail around the sand linga made by Sita in a vain attempt to remove it, and who was told to worship here to be freed of that offence. A third story tells that the aerial chariot of Indrajit was halted above the tower until he bathed in the tank.
sections.festivals: Festivals follow the Tamil calendar and are observed in the manner of a village Shiva temple. Vinayaka Chaturthi falls in the month of Aavani, in August or September, and Skanda Shashti with the annabhishekam, the bathing of the linga in cooked rice, in Aippasi, in October or November. Tirukarthigai is kept in Karthigai, Maha Shivaratri in Masi, and Panguni Uthiram in March or April, with the monthly Pradosham. Confirm dates locally, as sources differ and the temple does not publish a fixed calendar.
sections.experience: This is a quiet village temple, away from the crowds of the larger shrines, and it suits those who wish to pray without hurry. Many devotees come with a particular regret, a quarrel, or a mistake they have never been able to set right, and ask the Lord who forgives faults to release them from it. Stand before the linga, walk around the shrines in the corridors, and sit awhile by the Indra tirtham; the place invites a certain stillness. The temple may be in a phase of renovation, so check locally before travelling.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning until midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; published timings differ between sources, so confirm locally before travelling, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thalainayar lies about 12 km from Mayiladuthurai, and roughly 9 to 10 km from Vaitheeswaran Koil, which is the nearest railway station; Sirkazhi is about 15 to 18 km away. A bus from Mayiladuthurai toward Manalmedu passes through the village, but bus services on the last stretch are limited, so many visitors hire an auto or taxi. The nearest major airport is Tiruchirappalli, a long road journey away.
